posts.image_prompt: A heavy weathered grey stone slab lying among the tangled roots of a freshly uprooted tree on a late-1890s Minnesota farm field, faint carved marks on its face, a farmer in overalls looking down at it, autumn light
posts.caption:
🪨 DID VIKINGS REACH MINNESOTA IN 1362?

In 1898, Swedish immigrant farmer Olof Ohman was clearing trees on his land near Kensington, Minnesota. Tangled in the roots, he said, was a stone slab carved with runes.

The inscription claimed that a party of Swedes and Norwegians had travelled there in 1362 and suffered a tragedy.

If real, it would rewrite American history. It was even displayed at the Smithsonian in 1948–49.

But experts who studied the runes in 1899 found too many oddities in form and vocabulary for 14th-century Scandinavian. Most scholars since have agreed. In 1958, scholar Erik Wahlgren concluded it was a deliberate fraud, and in 1974 a confession by a local man, John Gran, to his children came to light, saying it was carved as a joke.

Today it sits in a museum in Alexandria, Minnesota — and still has believers.

Why do you think hoaxes like this are so hard to kill?

posts.caption:
🪙 Insert coin. Receive holy water. Around 2,000 years ago.

Hero of Alexandria described a coin-operated dispenser for temples: the coin's weight tipped a lever that briefly opened the flow.

What modern gadget do you think the ancients would have loved? 👇

posts.topic: Cahokia, the city of the mounds
posts.image_prompt: A vast ancient Native American city at sunrise with a huge terraced earthen mound topped by a large thatched wooden building, smaller mounds and thatched houses spreading across a river floodplain, smoke from cooking fires, cinematic wide aerial view
posts.caption:
🏞️ NORTH AMERICA'S FORGOTTEN CITY

Near modern St. Louis, Illinois, lie the remains of Cahokia — once the largest Native American city north of Mexico.

People settled here around 600 AD. From the 9th century they began building huge earthen mounds. At least 120 once stood here, and about 80 survive today.

The largest, Monks Mound, rises in terraces and was the city's focal point.

How many people lived here at its height? Estimates vary widely — from around 15,000 in the central city to as many as 40,000 by some counts. By some estimates, that rivaled London at the time.

Then, by around 1350, the city was abandoned. Researchers suggest drought or floods, political turmoil, or strain on food supplies. Nobody knows for sure.

Why do you think Cahokia isn't better known?

posts.caption:
🧊 ON THIS DAY in 1854, The Times carried explorer John Rae's report on the fate of the lost Franklin Expedition.

In 1845, 129 men sailed for the Arctic on HMS Erebus and HMS Terror and never came home. A note left in a cairn in 1848 said the ships had been abandoned in the ice and Franklin was already dead.

More than 30 search expeditions failed to find the ships. Then Erebus was discovered in 2014 and Terror in 2016.

We still don't fully know how the men died. What do you think went wrong? 👇

posts.topic: Archbishop Ussher's date for creation, 4004 BC
posts.caption:
📅 ON THIS DAY, according to a famous 17th-century calculation, the world began: October 23, 4004 BC.

The date came from James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh in Ireland and one of the most respected scholars of his time.

In 1650 he published a vast chronology, the Annales Veteris Testamenti. He added up the generations and reigns listed in the Old Testament, and anchored them to a known date in Babylonian history: 562 BC.

His answer: creation began at nightfall before Sunday, October 23, 4004 BC — near the autumn equinox, which he worked out using Johannes Kepler's astronomical tables.

He wasn't the only one trying. Bede had suggested 3952 BC. Kepler himself came up with 3992 BC.

Ussher's date was widely accepted in the Western world until the 19th century, and was printed in popular Bibles. Then geology revealed an Earth far older than anyone had imagined.

Even so, the scientist Stephen Jay Gould defended Ussher as a serious scholar for his age.

Should we judge thinkers of the past by what they could know then, or by what we know now?

posts.title: Galloping Gertie: The Bridge That Shook Itself Apart in 1940

scenes.narration: On the morning of November 7, 1940, a brand-new bridge in Washington State began to twist like a ribbon in the wind. And cameras were rolling.
scenes.label: 7 NOV 1940

scenes.narration: Within about an hour, its centre span had torn loose and plunged into Puget Sound. The bridge had been open for just four months and seven days.
In this film: the design choice that saved millions and doomed the bridge, the reporter who crawled for his life, and the myth physics textbooks still repeat.
The bridge crossed the Tacoma Narrows, a strait of Puget Sound. Construction began in November 1938.
Engineer Clark Eldridge's original design was estimated at 11 million dollars. Then the famous New York engineer Leon Moisseiff proposed changes.
Instead of 25-foot-deep stiffening trusses under the road, Moisseiff used solid steel plate girders only eight feet deep. His version cost about four million dollars less.
scenes.label: 8 FEET

scenes.narration: The result was elegant, slim and light. Its 2,800-foot main span made it the third-longest suspension bridge in the world.
scenes.label: 2,800 FEET

scenes.narration: On July 1, 1940, around 10,000 people came to the opening. But even before then, workers had noticed the deck moving up and down in the wind.
scenes.label: 1 JUL 1940

scenes.narration: They nicknamed it Galloping Gertie. The narrow, shallow deck simply moved too easily. Tie-down cables were added in October to steady it.
At the University of Washington, Professor Frederick Farquharson studied a model in a wind tunnel. He proposed fixes, but his studies finished only five days before the collapse.
image_search: Tacoma Narrows Bridge model wind tunnel

scenes.narration: On November 7, the wind blew from the southwest, striking the deck side-on. At around 9:30 a.m., engineers measured 42 miles per hour, up from 38 two hours earlier.
scenes.label: 42 MPH

scenes.narration: At about 10:03, the motion changed. The deck stopped bouncing and began to twist. Officials and state police closed the bridge.
Within minutes, the roadway was tilting up to 28 feet on each side, at angles of up to 45 degrees, roughly every five seconds.
scenes.label: 45 DEGREES

scenes.narration: Newspaper editor Leonard Coatsworth was out on the span in his car, with his daughter's cocker spaniel, Tubby, in the back seat.
The tilting deck threw his car against the curb. He climbed out of a window and made his way back to safety, but Tubby was still inside.
Around 10:55, Professor Farquharson himself went out to rescue the dog. The frightened dog bit him, and he had to retreat. Photographer Howard Clifford had already tried and turned back.
At 11:02 a.m., a 600-foot section of the centre span broke free, flipped over and fell 195 feet into the water. Spray shot more than 100 feet high.
By 11:10, it was over. Coatsworth's car and Tubby went down with the roadway. Tubby was the only life lost.
The collapse was filmed by Barney Elliott and Harbine Monroe of a local camera shop. In 1998, that footage was added to the U.S. National Film Registry.
scenes.label: FILMED

scenes.narration: Many physics textbooks call this a classic example of resonance. Engineers now say that is wrong. It was aeroelastic flutter: the wind fed the twisting, and the twisting caught more wind.

The solid, shallow girders acted like sails. The bridge was simply not stiff or heavy enough to resist the forces the wind created. That morning, the tie-down cables failed too. The disaster ended Moisseiff's career, and he died less than three years later.

A replacement bridge opened in 1950, reusing the old tower foundations and cable anchorages. The fallen deck still lies below, now an artificial reef listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
A cheaper design, a warning ignored, and a disaster caught on film. Who do you think was most to blame? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🌉 It was open for just four months — then it twisted itself apart on camera.

On November 7, 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State began swaying and twisting in a 40-mph wind. By 11:10 a.m., its centre span was at the bottom of Puget Sound.

This documentary covers the cost-cutting design, the nickname "Galloping Gertie", the editor who escaped on foot, the dog who didn't — and the physics myth textbooks still get wrong.

Who do you think was most to blame?
